title: A common summand for two surjections of finite free modules over a local ring
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative local ring, meaning a commutative ring with exactly one maximal ideal. Let $m,n\geq0$ be integers and let $\alpha,\beta:R^{\oplus n}\to R^{\oplus m}$ be surjective $R$-linear maps, where $R^{\oplus t}$ is the module of $t$-tuples with componentwise operations [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. There exists an $R$-submodule $U\subseteq R^{\oplus n}$ such that the restrictions $\alpha|_U:U\to R^{\oplus m}$ and $\beta|_U:U\to R^{\oplus m}$ are both isomorphisms. In particular $R^{\oplus n}=\ker(\alpha)\oplus U=\ker(\beta)\oplus U$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph: auxiliary common-summand assertion over a local ring, obtained by lifting a simultaneous complement from the residue field.

proof.text: Let $\mathfrak m$ be the unique maximal ideal and $k=R/\mathfrak m$. This quotient is a field: for $a\notin\mathfrak m$, maximality gives $1=ra+b$ with $b\in\mathfrak m$, so $\bar r\bar a=1$. Reduction is a local ring homomorphism $\rho:R\to k$, since its inverse image of the maximal ideal $0$ of $k$ is $\mathfrak m$. Reducing the coefficients of $\alpha,\beta$ in the standard bases gives $k$-linear maps $a,b:k^n\to k^m$. Both are surjective: lift a target vector coordinatewise to $R^m$, choose a preimage under the corresponding original surjection, and reduce that preimage. Put $V=k^n$, $A=\ker a$ and $B=\ker b$. The case $m=0$ already has the solution $U=0$; the following argument also covers it.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph; details supplied for the residue-field construction and its lift

proof.text: We first construct a simultaneous complement over $k$. Apply [lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement] to $C=A\cap B$ inside $A$ and inside $B$, obtaining $A=C\oplus A_0$ and $B=C\oplus B_0$. Apply it also to $A+B$ inside $V$, obtaining $V=(A+B)\oplus D$. Every subspace $P$ of $V$ is finite-dimensional: choose its complement using the same lemma and project the finite standard spanning family of $V$ onto $P$; the images span $P$. Thus all subspaces just named are finite-dimensional.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph; details supplied for the residue-field construction and its lift

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-idempotent-charpoly-rank-nullity] applied to $a$ and $b$, $\dim A+m=n=\dim B+m$, hence $\dim A=\dim B$. Apply that same theorem to the projections $A\to A_0$ and $B\to B_0$ along $C$, whose kernels are $C$, to obtain $\dim A_0+\dim C=\dim A=\dim B=\dim B_0+\dim C$. Therefore $\dim A_0=\dim B_0$. By [lem-trf-equal-dimension-linear-equivalence] choose a linear isomorphism $\theta:A_0\to B_0$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph; details supplied for the residue-field construction and its lift

proof.text: The sum $A+B=C\oplus A_0\oplus B_0$ is direct. Indeed if $c+x+y=0$ with $c\in C$, $x\in A_0$, $y\in B_0$, then $y=-c-x\in A\cap B=C$, so $y=0$ and then $c=x=0$. Consequently every vector of $V$ has unique coordinates $c+x+y+d$ in $C,A_0,B_0,D$. Define $G=\{x+\theta(x):x\in A_0\}$ and $\overline U=G+D$. This is a subspace by linearity of $\theta$, and its elements have unique expressions $x+\theta(x)+d$. The displayed decompositions justify these assertions directly, without a dimension count.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph; details supplied for the residue-field construction and its lift

proof.text: The subspace $\overline U$ is complementary to both $A$ and $B$. For $v=c+x+y+d$, put $z=\theta^{-1}(y)$; then $v=(c+x-z)+(z+\theta(z)+d)$ lies in $A+\overline U$. Also $v=(c+y-\theta(x))+(x+\theta(x)+d)$ lies in $B+\overline U$. If $x+\theta(x)+d\in A$, the unique coordinates force $d=0$ and $\theta(x)=0$, so $x=0$. Membership in $B$ similarly forces $d=x=0$. Thus $a|_{\overline U}$ and $b|_{\overline U}$ are injective. They are surjective because $a,b$ are surjective and vanish on $A,B$, respectively: decompose any preimage using the corresponding direct sum. The inverse of $a|_{\overline U}$, followed by inclusion, is a linear map $q:k^m\to k^n$ with image $\overline U$, $aq=1$, and $bq$ an isomorphism. Linearity of the inverse follows by applying the injective linear map $a|_{\overline U}$ to the addition and scalar identities.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph; details supplied for the residue-field construction and its lift

proof.text: For each standard basis vector $e_j$ of $k^m$, choose a vector $v_j\in R^n$ reducing to $q(e_j)$. Define $s:R^m\to R^n$ by $s((r_j))=\sum_j r_jv_j$. Its reduction is exactly $q$. In the scalar extension of [def-weil-module-base-change], identify $R^t\otimes_R k$ with $k^t$ by $(r_i)\otimes c\mapsto(\rho(r_i)c)$; its inverse is $(c_i)\mapsto\sum_i e_i\otimes c_i$. The tensor relations verify the two composites on the standard generators and pure tensors. Under these identifications, the scalar extensions of $\alpha s,\beta s:R^m\to R^m$ are $aq$ and $bq$, respectively: evaluate on each $e_j\otimes1$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph; details supplied for the residue-field construction and its lift

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-local-free-base-change-reflects-iso] to the local homomorphism $\rho:R\to k$ and separately to $\alpha s$ and $\beta s$. Both source and target are the finite free module $R^m$, and their scalar extensions are isomorphisms by steps 5--6. Hence $\alpha s$ and $\beta s$ are isomorphisms over $R$. In particular $s$ is injective: $s(t)=0$ implies $(\alpha s)(t)=0$ and then $t=0$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph; details supplied for the residue-field construction and its lift

proof.text: Set $U=\operatorname{im}s\subseteq R^n$. The map $s:R^m\to U$ is an isomorphism, with inverse $s(t)\mapsto t$ by injectivity. Thus $\alpha|_U$ and $\beta|_U$ are isomorphisms because their composites with this parametrization are $\alpha s$ and $\beta s$. Finally, for either $\gamma=\alpha$ or $\beta$, write $x=(x-u)+u$ with $u=(\gamma|_U)^{-1}(\gamma x)$; then $x-u\in\ker\gamma$. If $u\in U\cap\ker\gamma$, injectivity of $\gamma|_U$ gives $u=0$. This proves both asserted direct-sum decompositions. All sums and maps above allow empty standard bases.
